title: The Readiness of the Heart and the Twofold Creation of Man
english: But the phrase 'my bones have grown old' has been placed erroneously thus: 'because I was silent,' these things, the 'my bones have grown old from crying out all day long.' Not 'my bones have grown worn out from crying out all day long,' but 'because I was silent from crying out all day long'; for before this they had the day which 'the sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) makes. And he was crying out, this indeed praying, and that indeed glorifying God who grants me the day. Since therefore I was silent from crying out all day long, my bones have grown worn out.

It has been said to us also before that 'bones' refers to the vigorous powers of the soul and the doctrines of piety. Just as these bones hold together the whole body—for from them even the veins and everything is suspended. It is therefore said: 'All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you?' (Ps 145:17); not that these bones have sensation or intellect. For they do not feel themselves when being ground. Therefore 'my bones have grown old' was received. When it was united to God, then it cried out all day long. But since silence received the cry, my bones have grown worn out.

And I have already said that the unceasing one saw all the sons of men (Ps 32:13), having been cast as 'to the foolish beasts' (Ps 104:25). These, therefore, he saw, the sons of men, from his ready dwelling-place (Ps 104:26). His dwelling-place is like his temple, the state of his being... his throne. This throne is ready and a dwelling-place... 'Your throne is ready from of old, and you are from the age' (Ps 102:25). The ready... about him as a king. And of his throne we take up the thought... it comes, and thus hearing of his temple, we receive him as ready along with it... as if manifesting the state of God, the majesty of God. A soul which does not... his dwelling-place is ready. And this is also possible; one becomes ready from the same participation to make room for God's presence; holiness is briefly produced in the one having it; for that one begins to progress... taking the participation.

A dwelling-place of God is not ready; rather, through progress, something small becomes great as it is measured by its being, and it becomes ready. It is said that the good thing itself is ready, as if one says, 'My heart is ready, O God'; for he who has a prepared heart is a temple of God, a ready dwelling-place for Him. And again: 'Has it not been announced to you, O man, what is good' (Micah 6:8) and what is pleasant, 'but to do justice and to love mercy and to be ready to walk with your Lord God'? And again: 'Pay attention with your ear to the preparation of their heart' (Psalm 103:5).

He looked upon all who dwell in the earth (Psalm 36:6). Others are those dwelling in the earth, apart from the sons of men; for those who have not kept the image, nor have become [earthly], dwell. But the sons of this kind of men do not dwell, but they reside. For He 'causes the sun to rise' (Matthew 5:45) as it is 'upon the good,' and so also 'upon the evil,' He surveys all the sons of men, and those dwelling [in the earth], even irrational animals; for He gives 'food to all flesh' (Psalm 145:16). He flies into a snare; for we do not say the sons of men and those dwelling in the earth are parallel [terms].

He who formed [man] alone [formed] their hearts. In the Scripture, the doing is distinguished from the fashioning; for God made man 'according to His image and likeness' (Genesis 1:26), but He formed the man from the 'dust from the ground' (Genesis 2:7). And Job indeed says both these things: 'Your hands have formed me and made me' (Job 10:8). If he says this word strictly, the inner man becomes [the result], but the outer is fashioned. And as it has been said: 'Remember that you formed me of clay' (Job 10:9). The verb of forming implies a difference; for the one doing is able and will desire to bring into being as parents bring into existence. In the previously read passages, we say that 'to become' differs from 'to be created'; just as to form is not entirely [the same] as itself. Listen then to what he says...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Shaping of the Heart
english: He says that the hearts were formed by God in all ways, but 'only alone'. The hearts were formed 'only alone' to join heart to heart in companionship.

They certainly differ, and though many possess them, they possess them with some difference. This indeed is also said in Proverbs: 'Just as faces are not alike to faces, so also the hearts of men' are not alike (Proverbs 27:19). It is therefore difficult to find two similar faces. Even if the myth of Polydeuces and Castor is told, it stands only as a myth. They say the hemispheres are signified by these two names. Therefore they say day by day, living in parts; for the hemispheres are thus: when one semicircle becomes under the earth, the other becomes over the earth, because the semicircles are dissimilar in their likeness. If indeed you cut a circle in the middle, the semicircles are dissimilar. Let that be a myth to me.

But let us grant that such men have also come to be. It is therefore difficult to join face to face in likeness. 'Just as faces are not alike to faces, so also the hearts of men' are not alike (Proverbs 27:19). For indeed 'no one knew the things of man except the spirit of the man which is in him' (1 Corinthians 2:11). If no one knew the things of man except the spirit in him, the things of men have been formed by God individually, each one.

Having formed there a kind of mixture, for he said that they do not fall to the more sensory [understanding], just as a potter forms clay, the hearts, he knows all their works; for since one knows works in a certain way, if from the [works] themselves. We also say at other times that one who understands mechanical works is able to judge whether the parts of the clock are well or not. And upon an image, therefore, heart does not join to heart. Therefore he alone is called 'the knower of hearts of all' according to the prayer sent up by the apostles, when the disciples were making a selection. No one else is able to [know] the heart of...

[A man to] see. Therefore, one cannot separate heart from heart. And Job says, 'He who understands the mind of men' (Job 33:32). Even if another stood by... this [is] of God. He alone shapes the hearts. Each heart... the name of the shaping does not mean the creation of the heart... and indeed the elders, receiving its right which he... have said, 'Good is the shaping of your heart.' They do not say the essence of the heart is good, but the shaping, by which he skillfully worked. Toward the beautiful, he says, it has become... and it is possible to say by a second sense that the 'shaping of the heart' is then good, when it is protected from wickedness or ignorance, as it was in the beginning.

The man having become 'in the image and likeness' (Gen 1:26) of God is not said to have been shaped, but to have been made. But the man having become from clay and matter is said to be a shaping of God: 'Remember that you formed me of clay' (Job 10:9). And concerning both of the active powers of God it is said, 'Your hands shaped me and made me' (Ps 138:7). To fashion the heart... is a shaping of the heart, not to sustain it. So that you may know: the first making of our hearts had no difference; therefore it was not said then that each heart was shaped alone. There was no difference from the others. Here this is said after the subtext.

Regarding: 'one heart and one soul' (Acts 4:32) of the disciples? According to this, 'of those believing' according to being of one mind; for we do not take the whole from all. Regarding: so will the shaping ever cease? —the shaping alone, since this also took a beginning from us. And it took the beginning from us and an end it will reach, when it becomes—just as the Father and the Son are one (John 17:21), so all rational things are. I want it to be in this: 'that just as I and you are one, Father, so may we all be one' (John 17:21). Regarding: does making differ from creation? —it differs. To make signifies bringing into being from non-being, not to fashion; and for some, the name of creation also denotes the adornment of that which has become. The name of creation suffices even for the soulless: 'making...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: God's Creation and Transformation of Evil
english: “[He is] peace and one who creates [new things out of] evils.” And according to what is at hand, we say this: He proves to be a providential one over all things, and he gives peace to them and creates [new things out of] the evils. And in another way the expression was made clear to us thus: he creates evils as if it were an unclean creation, so that it might no longer be unclean; he creates, so that it might become pure, and he creates the two into one new man within him. He creates evils so that they might no longer be evils; for example, he creates evil men so that they might no longer be evil.

Question: regarding the quality? —the quality in the sense of being like it; “for we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph 2:10). Regarding the workmanship, he has not said “for good works,” but rather for the sake of being. But they are created “for good works,” so that they might do good works. Question: so that the formation is from the quality? —in such a way as is possible; for the essence was formed from the heart. And the heart is the mind.

And the name of creation is extended even to the sensible things: “and having created the world out of formless matter.” Question: regarding the rational [things] by analogy? —yes, regarding the rational in general. An extension is also found regarding the irrational souls, [the one] understanding all their works. He understands the works, because he knows the heart, and the beginnings of the happening works are taken from perception.

Among us, many receive men from what is within them; and those becoming imitators of God do so for no other reason than that “it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35); for giving is like God, but receiving is not; for each of those receiving is a recipient of something. But being a recipient is a deficiency, and that is to say, the saying that it is good “to give rather than to receive.”

Again: “blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy” (Matt 5:7). There is a certain lesser progress here; for in order to receive mercy, one must show mercy. Another, out of compassion, shows mercy, fearing that a man being so might fall into such [states]. Thus also Christians, out of compassion, nourish those in prison. Others again, having seen someone sometimes struck by disease, pity him because he has become ill. And again others do this even for the sake of the pursuit of glory, so that they might be glorified. But each of these, not being perfect, receives the more and the less; for the perfect is only that which does not [seek]...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
